title: The Bathymetry
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of loneliness and being seen
excerpt: The first ping came at 04:17 on the second night. At three thousand one hundred and forty meters, on a section of sea floor over which no ship had passed in sixty years. It was rectangular. It was twelve meters wide and eighteen long. It had three regular perpendicular structures along its length. Every subsequent night, it was closer.

chapters.title: Three Thousand One Hundred Forty
chapters.body:
The first ping came at 04:17 on the second night.

Dr. Cora Vance was in the small cabin she used as an office aboard the R/V Meridian Trawl, a converted fishing vessel refitted the previous decade for oceanographic work in the North Atlantic, when the sonar operator on watch — a young Portuguese technician named Rui whose English was still uncertain in matters not concerning sonar — knocked on her door and told her, in his careful way, that there was something she should see.

She had not been sleeping. She had been reviewing the previous day's data, cross-referencing the wide-swath multibeam readings from the Charlie transect against a set of older charts prepared by the American Navy in 1968, and she had been thinking, in the quiet way one thought at four in the morning on a small ship far from shore, about her marriage. She was forty-six. She had been divorced for nine months. She was not, at four in the morning on the second night of a three-week research cruise, particularly present.

She had said, without looking up: *what is it, Rui.*

Rui had said: *there is a return. At three thousand one hundred and forty meters. It is not on the chart.*

Cora had looked up.

She had been an oceanographer for twenty-two years. She had spent seven of those years, at various points, at sea. She had, in the course of those seven years, seen many returns on many sonars that were not on charts. Charts were incomplete. The sea floor was, even after seventy years of systematic mapping, one of the least-charted surfaces available to human science. A return not on a chart was, in general, not a matter of urgency.

She had looked at Rui.

Rui was not, she saw, treating this as a routine finding.

She had said: *show me.*

She had followed him along the narrow corridor to the sonar station, in her sock feet and her cardigan, at four-nineteen in the morning of the second night of the cruise, and she had, in the small blue light of the sonar operator's console, looked at what he was showing her.

The screen showed the multibeam return from a strip of sea floor along the Charlie transect, at a depth of three thousand one hundred and forty meters. The transect had been running for three hours. It had, until 04:17, produced a steady clean return of the kind Cora had expected: gently rolling abyssal plain with occasional low relief, the sediment record of the last several thousand years quietly accumulating on the bones of the last several million.

At 04:17 the return had changed.

There was, on the screen, a shape.

It was a rectilinear shape. It was, roughly, twelve meters wide and — Cora counted, on the small side scale of the display — perhaps eighteen meters long. It had, along its length, three regular perpendicular structures, evenly spaced. It had, at what appeared to be its forward end, a small squared projection.

It was not a whale. It was not a shipwreck. It was, in a way she had not, in twenty-two years of looking at sonar returns, quite seen before, *rectangular*.

She had looked at Rui.

Rui had said: *I do not know what it is.*

She had said: *neither do I.*

She had said, after a moment: *how far off the transect?*

He had said: *directly on. We are passing over it now.*

She had looked at the ship's position display. The R/V Meridian Trawl was, at that moment, at 52° 14' N, 32° 07' W, in the deep water of the North Atlantic well east of the Grand Banks, in a section of the sea floor over which she had personally selected the transect line three days earlier, in her cabin, from a chart on her laptop. She had chosen this line because it was empty. She had wanted, for the second night of the cruise, a clean baseline of undisturbed abyssal plain, against which the more interesting seamount structures further west would show up in relief. She had chosen a section that, according to every chart she had consulted, contained absolutely nothing.

She had stood in the small blue light of the sonar console and had watched, on the screen, the rectangular return pass slowly beneath the ship and vanish, and she had thought, with the clarity that came at that hour of the morning:

*I have made an error.*

—

She had, by six in the morning, ruled out four things.

She had ruled out a shipwreck. The shape was too regular. Ships did not lie on the sea floor at three thousand meters in perfectly rectangular outlines with three evenly-spaced cross-braces. Even the most rectangular of ships — barges, container hulls — deformed on the way down, buckled at the ribs, listed on the bottom. This had not deformed. This had, so far as the sonar could tell, come to rest on the abyssal plain with the geometric composure of a filing cabinet.

She had ruled out a lost container. Container ships did lose containers. Containers did, occasionally, sink to great depths and lie on the sea floor. But a container was six meters or twelve meters long, not eighteen. And a container did not have three evenly spaced perpendicular structures along its length. And a container did not appear on a section of sea floor over which no shipping lane had passed in the last sixty years.

She had ruled out a submarine. She had ruled it out because it was rectangular. Submarines were cigars. Submarines were not filing cabinets.

She had ruled out a geological feature. She had ruled this out last, and most reluctantly, because the sea floor did occasionally produce shapes that looked artificial. Basalt columns. Salt domes. Certain kinds of hydrothermal chimney. But those shapes were pillars, or cones, or clusters. None of them was a rectangle. None of them had perpendicular cross-braces at even intervals.

She had sat in her office at six in the morning with her second cup of coffee and had, systematically, ruled out every category of object that could reasonably be expected to appear at that location, and she had been left, at six-fifteen, with a screen full of ruled-out categories and no explanation for what she had seen.

She had, at six-thirty, when the ship's captain had come down to check on the night's progress, said nothing about the return.

She had thought about this decision later, and had not, on reflection, been quite able to justify it. It had not been a conscious decision. She had simply, when the captain had asked *any interesting overnight,* said, *nothing to report, an ordinary transect,* and had turned back to her data. She had not lied. She had, more precisely, elided. She had not wanted, at six-thirty in the morning, to open the question of the rectangular return with a man who would, quite reasonably, want to know how far it was from the nearest working shipping lane and whether they should notify anyone, and she had not wanted to notify anyone, and she had not wanted, still less, to explain to herself why she did not want to notify anyone.

She had, she noticed later, been protecting it.

She had, at six-thirty on the second morning, already begun to think of the rectangular return as *hers.*

—

She had run the transect again on the third night.

She had done this without formally announcing the reason. She had told the captain, at dinner on the third day, that the previous night's Charlie transect had shown some anomalies in the sediment layer that she wanted to verify, and she had asked whether they could re-run the same line on the second overnight watch. The captain, a Danish man named Lars who trusted her because they had worked together twice before, had said of course.

She had been in the sonar station at 03:00.

She had told Rui to go get some sleep. She had said she would take the watch. Rui had looked at her — he was not, she thought, entirely deceived, but he was young enough not to press — and had gone.

She had sat alone at the console.

At 04:17 the ship had crossed 52° 14' N, 32° 07' W.

The shape had come up again.

It was in exactly the same place. It was, so far as the sonar could tell, exactly the same shape. Twelve meters by eighteen. Three cross-braces. The small squared projection at the forward end. She had, this time, had the presence of mind to save the raw return to her personal data drive, along with the precise coordinates and the timestamp, and she had, when the shape had passed beneath the ship and disappeared, sat very still in the small blue light of the sonar station.

She had reached forward. She had checked the depth of the return.

It was at three thousand one hundred and thirty-six meters.

It was, in other words, four meters shallower than it had been on the second night.

She had sat in the console chair for a long time.

She had thought about the tolerances of multibeam sonar at three thousand meters depth. She had thought about the accuracy of positioning of the ship at 52° 14' N, 32° 07' W, and about how much drift was possible in a return over a twenty-four-hour period. She had thought about whether a four-meter difference in a bottom return at three thousand meters depth was within the noise floor of the measurement.

It was, at the outside, within the noise floor. It was at the very edge of what she could reasonably attribute to instrument error.

But the shape had also been exactly the same shape. And the shape had also been at exactly the same coordinates. And the shape had also had, when she zoomed in, exactly the same three cross-braces, in exactly the same positions, and the exactly the same small squared projection at the forward end.

Everything else about the return had been identical.

Except the depth.

She had, in her office at four-thirty in the morning of the third day, opened a small blank document on her laptop and had begun a private log.

She had titled the document *charlie-anomaly.txt*.

At the top of the document she had written:

*Night 2. 04:17. 52° 14' N, 32° 07' W. Depth 3,140 m. Shape approx. 12 x 18 m, rectangular, three cross-braces, forward squared projection. Not on chart.*

*Night 3. 04:17. Same coordinates. Depth 3,136 m. Same shape.*

She had looked at what she had written.

She had thought: *it moved.*

She had thought: *it moved four meters up.*

She had thought, with a small precise coldness: *this is not what I have been trained to do.*

She had gone on writing, all the same:

*Nights 4-5: request approval from captain to run Charlie transect again. Pretext: sediment layer verification (continuing).*

She had, she noted afterwards, not written down her hypothesis. She had not needed to. It was, at four-thirty in the morning of the third day, already sitting in her mind with the quiet permanence of a fact.

Something at three thousand meters was rising.

—

She had run the transect again on the fourth night.

The shape had been at three thousand one hundred and thirty meters. Six meters shallower than the second night. Two meters shallower than the third.

She had run the transect on the fifth night. Three thousand one hundred and twenty-two meters.

She had run it on the sixth night. Three thousand one hundred and ten meters.

She had understood, on the sixth night, that whatever was rising was rising at an accelerating rate. Between nights two and three it had risen four meters. Between five and six it had risen twelve. The rate was increasing. If it continued at this pace it would, she had calculated in her office on the sixth night with her second coffee cold in her hand, breach the surface within eleven days.

She had sat in her office with her laptop open in front of her.

She had thought about what she was going to do.

She had thought about telling the captain. She had rehearsed this conversation. *Lars, there is something rising off the abyssal plain at 52° 14' N, 32° 07' W. It is rectangular. It is twelve by eighteen meters. It has three cross-braces. It has been rising at an accelerating rate for four nights. It will breach the surface in approximately eleven days. I have not, so far, told anyone. I would like your advice about who to tell.*

She had imagined Lars's face.

She had imagined the calls that would follow. The Woods Hole director. The Bermuda station. The Navy. The Navy above all, because a rectangular twelve-by-eighteen-meter object rising off the abyssal plain of the North Atlantic was, whatever else it was, a matter of interest to the Navy. She had imagined the ship being ordered to remain on station. She had imagined the arrival, within days, of a research vessel with rather better equipment than the Meridian Trawl, and rather more personnel, and rather more authority. She had imagined the whole of her small quiet three-week cruise being taken from her, and being replaced with something official, something loud, something bright.

She had imagined the object being taken from her.

She had, once again, noticed her own protective feeling toward it.

She had sat in the small cabin at four-thirty on the sixth morning and had understood, with a small clarity that she had not, in nine months of divorce and twenty-two years of a professional life, expected to feel again: she was going to see this through alone.

She had opened the *charlie-anomaly.txt* document.

She had added, at the bottom:

*Night 6. Continuing observation. Not yet reported. Rationale: —*

She had stopped there. She had sat and had looked at the empty space after the em-dash, and had, after some time, closed the file without finishing the sentence.

She had gone to bed. She had slept, for the first time on the cruise, deeply and without dreams, and she had woken at ten in the morning to a bright cold day and the sound of a herring gull calling somewhere astern, and she had, in that first waking moment before she had remembered what she was doing, felt more herself than she had felt in nine months.

chapters.title: The Rise
chapters.body:
By the tenth night the object was at two thousand nine hundred meters.

It had risen, in eight days, two hundred and forty meters. The rate of ascent had continued to accelerate — between nights nine and ten it had risen forty-eight meters — and Cora, in her office, with the small precise handwriting she had used for her graduate notebooks, had begun to plot the ascent on graph paper by hand, because there was something in the plotting by hand that felt right to her, some old careful ritual of scientific attention that she had not performed in many years.

The curve was, unmistakably, exponential.

If she projected the curve forward, the object would reach the surface — or, more precisely, would rise into the region of open water where surface effects began — in five nights. Perhaps four. She had, on the tenth morning, checked the projection three times, at three different levels of precision, and had produced three answers that agreed with each other to within twelve hours.

She had noted this in her log. She had then closed the log, and had gone up to the deck, and had stood at the port rail for some time looking at the ocean.

The North Atlantic in mid-October was grey. The waves that morning were moderate — perhaps three meters — with a low overcast that lit the water evenly from horizon to horizon and gave it the appearance of a single flat pewter surface, without depth or feature. Cora had looked at the water. She had thought about how many meters of water were between her and the object. She had thought about how thin, in some perspectives, three thousand meters was. She had thought about how thick, in others, it was.

She had thought: *I am standing above it now.*

The ship had, of course, moved on from Charlie transect. The ship had, in the eight days since the first return, run through the Delta and Echo transects and part of Foxtrot, and was now well to the west of the point where the object lay. But Cora had, over the last week, developed a strange awareness of the object's position relative to the ship, which persisted whether or not the ship was above it. She always knew where it was. She could have pointed to it. She could have said, at any moment of any day, *it is that way, at that distance, at that depth,* and been within a mile of correct.

She had, she thought, been building up this awareness for a week.

She had been building it in the same way one built up an awareness of a person one was in love with in the early stages — a low background attention that ran under everything else, tracking, always tracking, where the other party was in space and time.

She had noted this comparison in her private notebook, in the small evening hours when she wrote for herself, and had underlined it, and then had crossed it out.

She had not, since her divorce, made any comparisons of this kind about anything, and she was not, on the tenth morning of the cruise, entirely comfortable with the comparison having arisen.

She had gone back down to her cabin.

—

She had begun, on the eleventh day, to consider the possibility of getting closer.

There was, aboard the R/V Meridian Trawl, an ROV. It was a small remotely operated vehicle, tethered to the ship by an armored cable, with a rated depth of three thousand five hundred meters. It carried two forward cameras and a spotlight, and it could, at the operator's discretion, hold station at a given depth and coordinate for extended observation. It had been brought on the cruise for the seamount survey scheduled for the third week. It was, at present, sitting in its cradle on the aft deck.

Cora had been trained on its operation. She was one of two people aboard the ship who could operate it. The other was a young technician named Andreas, who was, at present, ashore in Ponta Delgada with a family emergency, and would not be joining the cruise until the third week.

If Cora chose to run the ROV, she would have to justify running it to the captain. She would have to justify it against the scheduled use of the ship's time. She would have to explain, in some form, what she wanted to look at.

She had thought about this on the eleventh morning, and had rehearsed a version of the conversation. She had rehearsed it, and had rejected it, and had rehearsed it again, and had rejected it again, and had, in the end, decided that she was not going to have the conversation. She was going to wait.

She was going to wait, she understood, because she wanted the object to come to her.

She wanted to be at the surface, in the small dim light of a cold overcast morning, when it broke through.

She wanted to be the one who saw it.

She had written this, in her private notebook, on the evening of the eleventh day:

*I want to be the one who sees it. I do not want to send a machine to look at it early. I want it to come.*

She had read what she had written.

She had thought about the woman who had written it. This woman was, in ways she could not immediately name, not the woman she had been three weeks earlier. Three weeks earlier she had been a scientist. Three weeks earlier she had been an oceanographer whose primary interest in the sea floor was the sediment record and whose primary emotional state was a low quiet grief about a marriage she had ended. Three weeks earlier she would not have considered, for a single hour, protecting an anomalous sonar return from her captain.

The woman who had written *I want it to come* was, however, unmistakably her.

She had thought, at the small desk in her cabin at nine o'clock on the eleventh evening: *this is what the object is doing to me.*

She had thought: *it is not doing it. I am doing it. It is offering, and I am accepting.*

She had thought, and this thought had come with a small warmth she had not felt since her twenties: *I have been waiting to be able to do this for many years.*

She had closed the notebook. She had gone to bed. She had slept badly, and had dreamed, when she had slept, of a flat pewter ocean under a low grey sky, and of a shape rising slowly through the water beneath her, and of the moment — she had woken at this moment — when she had understood that the shape was aware that she was above it and was rising to meet her.

—

On the twelfth night she broke into the sonar system.

She did not, in the end, need to break in. She had access. She had, as principal investigator, the access to override the sonar operator's watch schedule and to run bespoke transects at her discretion, and she had, on the twelfth evening, exercised this access to run a short high-resolution transect over the object's current position.

The object had been at two thousand seven hundred and forty meters.

It had risen, since the previous night, one hundred and sixty meters.

The rate had, in other words, accelerated further. Cora had, on her graph paper, added the new point. The curve was, if anything, steeper than exponential. It was, she thought, approaching something more like a hyperbola. If she extended the curve to the surface, she was going to run out of measurable depth in perhaps forty-eight hours.

The object was going to breach on the fourteenth night.

She had stood in the sonar station in the small blue light and had thought about this.

She had thought about the fact that on the fourteenth night the ship would, according to the planned itinerary, be over the seamount cluster three hundred nautical miles west of the Charlie transect. She had thought about how she was going to get the ship back to Charlie transect in time. She had thought about the story she was going to tell the captain to justify a three-day diversion.

She had realized, as she thought about it, that she was not going to be able to justify it.

The captain was going to say no.

The captain was going to say that a three-day diversion halfway through a three-week cruise, without more explanation than she had so far offered, was not an acceptable use of the ship's time. He was going to demand explanations. He was going to see her log, or he was going to insist she share the anomaly with the shore-side team, and either way the object was going to be taken from her.

Cora had, at that point, done a thing she had not done in twenty-two years of a scientific career.

She had lied.

She had gone to the captain the next morning and had told him that the sediment cores from the previous night's transect showed a striking anomaly of a type she had not, in her career, encountered before, and that she believed it warranted a return to the Charlie transect for a proper high-resolution survey. She had told him, further, that she believed the anomaly could contribute to a paper of some significance, and that she would credit him in the acknowledgments. She had said this last thing looking him in the eye, in the small officers' mess, over her second cup of coffee, and she had watched him weigh her.

He had said, after a moment: *how long.*

She had said: *three days on the transect. Two days back to the seamount work. Five days total off schedule.*

He had said: *the sponsor is expecting the seamount work.*

She had said: *I will explain to the sponsor. I will take the responsibility.*

He had looked at her for a long moment.

He had said, quietly: *Cora. Is everything all right.*

She had said, without hesitation: *yes.*

He had held her gaze another moment. She had, in that moment, understood that he had known she was lying — not about the details, not about the sediment anomaly, but about *something* — and that he was choosing, for reasons of his own, not to press her. Lars had known her for eleven years. He had been at her wedding. He had, over the course of those eleven years, seen her make many decisions, and he had, in general, trusted her.

He had said: *all right.*

He had turned the ship around that morning.

They had arrived back at the Charlie transect coordinates by dusk on the thirteenth day, and Cora had gone to her cabin and had lain on her bunk in the fading light and had felt, for the first time since the divorce, the specific sensation of being in exactly the right place at exactly the right time. The sensation was warm and quiet and absolute.

She had understood, lying on her bunk, that she was going to do whatever the object required of her.

She had understood, further, that she was going to do it willingly.

She had not asked herself, in the fading light of the thirteenth evening, why the object should be requiring anything of her. This question had not, at any point since the twelfth night, occurred to her. She had not needed to ask. She had known, in the way she had known where the object was in space, that the object had begun requiring things of her the moment she had, on the second night, said *nothing to report.*

The object had begun requiring things of her, and she had begun providing them, and this was the whole of the arrangement, and she had — she understood, lying in the fading light — she had been waiting to be part of an arrangement of this specific shape for her entire adult life.

chapters.title: Surface
chapters.body:
The fourteenth night was clear.

The weather had, over the last thirty-six hours, cleared unexpectedly — the low overcast that had been sitting over the eastern North Atlantic for the whole of the cruise had lifted on the morning of the thirteenth day, and by dusk on the fourteenth the sky was a deep pure black under a moon just past full, and Cora, standing at the port rail at eleven o'clock at night, could see, in the moonlight, the surface of the sea for miles.

The ship was on station.

Lars had, at Cora's request, brought the ship to a full stop at the Charlie coordinates at ten in the evening, with the engines idling, and had ordered the deck lights doused so as not to interfere with the surface observation Cora had claimed she wanted to make of the local bioluminescence. It was a reasonable pretext. It was also a lie. She had wanted the deck lights doused because she wanted, when the object came, to see it in the moonlight.

She was standing alone at the rail.

She had told Rui to take the sonar watch, and had told him to alert her the moment there was any return above two thousand five hundred meters. She had, therefore, a technical justification for standing at the rail — she was, ostensibly, watching for surface disturbance that might accompany a shallow bottom feature — but the truth was that she was watching because she wanted to.

She had, in the pocket of her cardigan, her private notebook. She had not opened it. She was not, at that moment, taking notes. She was — she understood herself with a strange precision at that moment — she was *waiting*, in the way one waited for a person one had once loved to come around a corner.

The sea in front of her was flat.

The North Atlantic was almost never flat. The North Atlantic was almost always heaving in some direction, with waves of at least a meter running from somewhere to somewhere else. But this night, on the fourteenth night of the cruise, at the Charlie coordinates in mid-October, the surface of the sea was as still as a pond in a garden.

Cora had looked at it for a long time.

She had thought: *it is waiting too.*

At eleven-forty Rui had come to the rail.

He had said: *Dr. Vance. There is a return.*

She had said: *how deep.*

He had said: *two thousand.*

She had said: *and rising.*

He had said: *yes.*

She had said: *stay on the sonar. Note the depths every five minutes. Do not tell the captain. Do not tell anyone.*

Rui had looked at her.

He had said, in his careful English: *Doctor. What is coming up.*

She had said: *I do not know. But it is coming up to me.*

Rui had looked at her for a moment longer. He had, she thought, been about to say something else — some small careful young man's protest, some request for clarification, some invocation of the protocols they were both, at that moment, in the process of violating. But he had not. He had, in the end, only nodded, and turned, and gone back below decks to the sonar console.

She had understood, watching him go, that he had, in his own way, been affected as she had been. That some part of the object's rising had, over the last two weeks, reached even into the small dim quiet of the sonar operator's chair, and had produced there a small young Portuguese man who was, at eleven-forty on the fourteenth night, willing to keep a secret.

She had turned back to the sea.

—

The object breached at twelve-oh-three.

There was, first, a small change in the surface of the water directly ahead of the ship — a low ripple, perhaps two meters across, that did not belong to any wave pattern that had been there before. Cora, watching, saw it. The ripple grew. It became a small round patch of water that was, for a moment, mounded up — a low dome, no more than half a meter high, but definite — and then the dome collapsed, and the water in the patch was, for a moment, dark.

Then something came out.

It came out slowly. It rose from the water without splash, without disturbance, without any of the violence Cora had, in some part of her mind, been expecting. It rose the way a candle rose out of its holder when one lifted the holder from below. It rose, straight up, from the black water, and it was — she saw it clearly in the moonlight, thirty meters from the ship's bow — it was rectangular.

Twelve meters wide.

Eighteen meters long.

Three regular perpendicular structures along its length.

A small squared projection at what she now saw was its forward end.

It was, she understood in the same first moment, black. Not the black of shadow. The black of an object that absorbed light. Even in the direct moonlight it seemed to reflect nothing — it stood in the water like an absence, a piece of missing space, the shape of a filing cabinet cut out of the world.

She stared at it.

It stood on the surface of the water.

It did not sink. It did not float. It did not do any of the things that objects on the surface of the water did. It stood, absolutely still, in the small patch of undisturbed water thirty meters from the bow of the R/V Meridian Trawl, and it was, so far as Cora could tell, aware that she was watching it.

She said, quietly, into the still air: *hello.*

The object did not move.

She said: *I saw you first.*

She had not planned to say this. It had come out of her without preparation, from somewhere below her thinking. She heard herself say it and had, for a moment, been surprised that she had said it, and then, in the second moment, had understood that it was the exact thing she had needed to say.

The object shifted.

It did not move. Nothing about its position changed. But it — she had no other word — it *turned its attention* to her. She felt it. She felt it as one felt, in a crowded room, the moment a specific stranger's gaze arrived on one's face. The object had, up to that moment, been coming up. It had, at that moment, arrived, and had, in its arrival, noticed her.

She was, she understood, being seen.

She had been being seen, in fact, for some time. Since the second night, perhaps. Since the moment she had said *nothing to report* in the small officers' mess at six-thirty on the second morning. Since the moment she had, without justification, chosen not to file the return. She had been in some form of relationship with the rectangular object for twelve days, and only now, at twelve-oh-three on the fourteenth night, had she stood in front of it and been directly looked at.

She stood at the rail.

She thought: *what do you want.*

She did not say it. She did not need to.

The object stood on the water. The moon on the water behind it made a small silver band that did not touch its edges. Somewhere below, in the sonar station, Rui was noting depths that were, presumably, now zero. Somewhere above, in the captain's quarters, Lars was sleeping.

The answer came into Cora's mind. It did not come as words. It came as a shape — a small definite understanding that landed in her, complete, the way a bird landed on a branch.

The understanding was: *I want the same thing you want.*

She stood at the rail.

She thought about this.

She thought about what she wanted.

She had not, for a long time, permitted herself to think about what she wanted. She had, after the divorce, made a small careful project of not wanting things, on the grounds that most of what she had wanted at various points in her life had turned out either to be impossible to have or to be, once had, insufficient. She had, over the last nine months, wanted her marriage back briefly, and had understood this to be impossible, and had put it away. She had, more distantly, wanted a certain kind of career recognition that had never quite arrived, and had, over the years, put that away too. She had, still more distantly, wanted a child, and had, at forty-two, understood that this was not going to happen, and had put that away.

She was, at forty-six, standing at the rail of a research vessel in the North Atlantic looking at an unidentified rectangular object that had risen from the abyssal plain to meet her, and she was being asked, by the object, what she wanted.

She thought, and this thought came from a place she had not consulted in many years:

*I want to matter.*

*I want to have mattered.*

She stood with the thought. She let it be there. She did not, this time, put it away.

The object stood on the water.

She understood, from the object, without words:

*You have. You do. To me.*

She did not know how to receive this. She did not know how to accept, at forty-six, on a research vessel in the North Atlantic, the specific gift of being told, by whatever this thing was, that she mattered to it.

She stood at the rail.

She began, quietly, to weep.

She wept without covering her face. She wept looking directly at the object, in the moonlight, with the still air of the North Atlantic on her cheek. She wept for a long time. She wept for the divorce and for the child she had not had and for the small careful woman she had made herself into over the last twenty years, and she wept for the way this small careful woman had, over those years, learned to accept smaller and smaller shapes of herself in order to fit the smaller and smaller shapes of the life available to her. She wept for the way she had come, gradually, without noticing, to believe that what she wanted was not important enough to require of the world.

The object stood on the water and let her weep.

It stood there until she was done.

—

At one-thirty in the morning it began to sink.

It went down as it had come up — straight, without splash, without disturbance. The rectangular black shape descended into the still water until only its top edge was visible, and then that too was gone, and the surface of the water where it had been was, once more, ordinary sea. The moon-band on the surface continued unbroken.

Cora stood at the rail.

She stood there for perhaps another half hour. She was, by then, not weeping. She was, she thought, resting.

At two in the morning she went below decks. She went to the sonar station. Rui was there. He looked at her.

She said, quietly: *what is the last depth.*

He said: *three thousand one hundred and forty meters.*

She said: *it went back.*

He said: *yes.*

She said: *good.*

He looked at her.

He said, in his careful English: *Dr. Vance. Are you well.*

She said: *yes.*

She said: *thank you, Rui. Please erase tonight's log.*

He said: *Doctor.*

She said: *please. All of it. Depths, timestamps, everything from ten o'clock onwards.*

He looked at her for a long moment.

He said: *and if the captain asks.*

She said: *he will not ask.*

She said: *and if he does, you tell him you were on the sonar and there was nothing to report.*

Rui looked at her. He was, she thought, very young. He was, she thought, going to spend the rest of his career on ships wondering what had happened on the fourteenth night of the R/V Meridian Trawl cruise in October, and he was, she thought, going to learn, over the course of that career, to keep his own secrets in the way she had learned to keep hers.

He said, quietly: *yes, Doctor.*

He turned to the console. He began, methodically, to erase.

She went to her cabin.

—

She finished the cruise.

She completed the seamount survey. She produced, on time, the technical report the sponsor had commissioned. She produced, in the following year, two papers on the sediment structure of the abyssal plain southeast of the Grand Banks. Neither paper mentioned any rectangular return. Neither paper mentioned the Charlie transect on the second night, or on any of the subsequent nights. Neither paper mentioned anything unusual at all.

She kept her private notebook.

She kept it for the rest of her life. She wrote in it, from time to time — not often, but from time to time — whenever the sensation returned to her of being looked at by the object. The sensation returned, on and off, for the next three decades. Sometimes it arrived when she was at home in her small apartment in Falmouth. Sometimes it arrived when she was at sea. Sometimes it arrived in the small quiet moments of an ordinary afternoon, in the middle of a walk, in the middle of a lecture, in the middle of a phone call with her sister.

She always knew what it was. She always knew, when it arrived, that the object was — somewhere in the North Atlantic, at some depth she could not have specified — thinking of her.

She was thinking of it, too.

She was often, in the last decades of her life, thinking of it.

She died at seventy-nine, of a stroke, in the small apartment in Falmouth, on a cold clear morning in March. Her sister came to clean out the apartment, and found, on the desk, a small black notebook, and did not, because Cora had left instructions to that effect in her will, read it. The notebook was, in accordance with the will, buried with her.

She was buried in the town cemetery in Falmouth, which is well inland, and does not smell of the sea.

If, however, one walks the cemetery at night in October, one may sometimes have the sensation, at the small headstone marked Cora Vance 1979–2058, that something very far away is thinking of her still. The sensation is small, and warm, and specific. It is the sensation of being known.

She would, if she could still receive it, have understood.
